headline: Approved legislative advocacy priorities; discussed possible $10 million state aid cut and legal options.
summary: The committee approved its legislative advocacy priorities and sent them to the full board. The state targeted aid cap is estimated to reduce state funding to Manchester by slightly more than $10 million a year. House Bill 1831, which sought to address that cap, was tabled.
decisions: Agreed to place further discussion and outreach on IDEA special education funding on the October agenda.
Tabled House Bill 1831, which sought to address the targeted aid cap affecting Manchester.
Approved legislative advocacy priorities and forwarded them to the full board; all were in favor and the motion passed.

plain_text:
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION LEGISLATION 
 
September 9, 2026 5:00 p.m.  
 
1. Chair O’Connell called the meeting to order at 5:00 p.m. 
 
2. The Clerk called the roll.  
 
Present: Committee Members O’Connell, Parr, Smith, Representative Chretien and 
Attorney Upton. 
 
  
 
3. Public Forum 
 
There was no one present wishing to speak. 
   
 
6.  Board of School Committee Legislative Advocacy Priorities – by Dr. Sean Parr   
 
Dr. Parr reviewed the Board of School Committee's legislative advocacy priorities, noting that the 
document has been reviewed and updated periodically over approximately the past four years. 
The Committee reviewed the following priority areas: 
1. Education Funding – Advocating for full and equitable funding of public education in New 
Hampshire and opposing legislation that diminishes funding available to the Manchester 
School District. 
2. Retirement Funding – Supporting an increase in the State's contribution toward teacher 
retirement costs. 
3. Pandemic-Related Learning Support – Supporting additional state funding to address 
learning impacts resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic. 
4. Targeted Funding – Advocating for increased support for schools and districts serving higher 
proportions of students experiencing poverty, English language learners, and students receiving 
special education services. 
5. IDEA Funding – Advocating for the federal government to meet its commitment to fund 40 
percent of the excess costs associated with special education. 
6. Student Support Funding – Supporting additional funding for student mental health, 
behavioral supports, MTSS-B, professional and technical education, alternative education 
programs, and other student services.

7. Food Insecurity – Supporting universal meals and Medicaid direct certification for free and 
reduced-price meals. 
8. Early Childhood Education – Supporting universal pre-kindergarten programming and 
related facility needs. 
9. Renewable Energy and Environmental Sustainability – Supporting incentives and funding 
opportunities for energy efficiency, renewable energy, electric school buses, and sustainability-
related building improvements. 
10. Assessment Reform – Supporting reductions in the number and impact of mandated 
standardized assessments and movement toward a more balanced assessment system that 
includes performance-based measures. 
11. Student Discipline Alternatives – Supporting state funding for alternatives to suspension and 
expulsion, including restorative practices and other intervention programs. 
 
The Committee discussed Medicaid direct certification for free and reduced-price meals and the 
potential effect of adopting a system that automatically qualifies eligible students rather than requiring 
families to complete a separate application. 
 
The Committee also discussed IDEA funding and the longstanding federal commitment to contribute 
40 percent of excess special education costs. Members discussed reaching out to federal candidates and 
members of the congressional delegation regarding this issue. The Committee agreed that further 
discussion and potential outreach should be placed on the October agenda. 
 
Early Childhood Education and Sustainability 
The Committee discussed the importance of early childhood education and the challenges families face 
because of the high cost of preschool and childcare. Members noted that increased access to universal 
pre-kindergarten could have a significant impact on students entering the public school system. 
Renewable energy and sustainability were also discussed. Members considered opportunities for the 
District to establish policies supporting long-term movement toward electric transportation, renewable 
energy, and energy efficiency. 
 
The Committee discussed the District's substantial building footprint and the potential future use of 
solar energy. It was noted that the current middle school renovation projects and the new Beech Street

School are being designed so that solar panels could potentially be added in the future if the District or 
City elects to pursue that option. 
 
Assessment Reform and Ed 306 Rules 
The Committee discussed the relationship between its assessment reform priority and the revised New 
Hampshire Ed 306 minimum standards.  It was clarified that changes to the Ed 306 rules did not alter 
required statewide assessments. Members discussed concerns regarding changes to minimum state 
education standards and noted that Manchester has continued to maintain standards beyond the 
minimum state requirements in several areas. 
 
Student Discipline Alternatives 
The Committee discussed its legislative priority of seeking state funding for alternatives to suspension 
and expulsion.  Attorney Upton reported that he is working with Executive Director of Safe and 
Supportive Schools Stacy Champey on the development of a student diversion program. The concept 
would provide certain students facing long-term suspension or expulsion with an opportunity to 
participate in a structured intervention program. 
 
Students participating in the proposed program would be required to enter into an agreement outlining 
specific expectations. Depending on individual needs, the program could include counseling, academic 
supports, regular clinician meetings, case management, and other services. An expulsion could be held 
in abeyance while a participating student successfully complies with the requirements of the program. 
The goal would be to address the underlying causes of student behavior while minimizing unnecessary 
loss of instructional time and reducing the likelihood that students return to school with greater 
behavioral or academic challenges. 
 
Attorney Upton noted that some students must be removed from school for legitimate safety reasons; 
however, he stated that other students may benefit significantly from structured supports and 
alternative pathways. 
 
The Committee discussed the possibility of calling the initiative the Manchester Student Diversion 
Program or Student Success Program, although no final name has been selected.
September 9, 2026 Committee on Education Legislation 
Page 4 of 7 
 
Attorney Upton also reported that alternative programming is being explored at Parkside Middle 
School and that additional student conduct policy revisions are being developed. The proposed changes 
would improve the District's ability to track disciplinary incidents and establish additional limitations 
regarding when out-of-school suspension is appropriate. 
 
Members discussed the educational consequences of removing students from school for conduct such 
as repeated tardiness and emphasized the importance of developing disciplinary responses that address 
behavior without unnecessarily increasing learning loss. 
 
Dr. Parr clarified that the legislative priority is intended primarily to seek state funding to support these 
programs. Existing grant funding, including Project AWARE funding, has helped support related 
work, but that funding is not permanent. 
 
Attorney Upton noted that diversion programs would likely require dedicated case managers or similar 
personnel to work individually with participating students and coordinate services. 
 
Legislative Updates 
Representative Creighton provided an update regarding several legislative matters.  House Bill 1831, 
which sought to address the targeted aid cap affecting Manchester, was tabled. Representative 
Creighton indicated that information developed in support of the bill had been provided to another 
legislator for possible continuation of the effort in the next legislative session. 
 
The Committee also discussed House Bill 1300 and uncertainty regarding how its budget-cap 
provisions could affect municipalities such as Manchester.  Attorney Upton reported that discussions 
had taken place regarding the potential application of HB 1300 to Manchester. Because Manchester 
already operates under a tax cap, the District may be required to calculate the impact under both 
provisions if the measure ultimately becomes applicable, with the more restrictive limitation 
potentially controlling. 
 
The Committee discussed the legislation's six-percent limitation on SAU administrative costs. Attorney 
Upton reported that Manchester's current administrative costs are approximately 4.5 percent of the 
District budget.

Representative Creighton reported that the Education Funding Committee was scheduled to meet on 
October 6 to consider a number of bills, including measures relating to: 
 School administrative unit budget caps; 
 Methods of increasing revenues for education; 
 A centralized enterprise resource planning service; 
 Reporting of foreign grants and donations by higher education institutions; 
 Recodification of education laws; 
 State education property tax and property-tax relief; 
 Catastrophic special education aid; and 
 A foundation opportunity budget program for public education. 
 
The Committee was advised that these matters had already gone through public comment and would 
be before the legislative committee for votes. 
 
On motion of Committee Member Parr, duly seconded by Committee Member Smith, it was moved to 
approve the Board of School Committee Legislative Advocacy Priorities, and forward this item to the 
full Board of School Committee for approval.  All were in favor and the motion passed. 
 
 
7.  Discussion regarding:  The State Targeted Aid Cap and Its Impact on Manchester –     
by Attorney Matt Upton  
 
The Committee next discussed the targeted aid cap and its anticipated financial impact on the 
Manchester School District.  Members reviewed legislation limiting differentiated or targeted aid to the 
first 5,000 qualifying students within a municipality. Because Manchester is the only municipality with 
a student population large enough to exceed that threshold, the practical impact is concentrated on 
Manchester. 
 
The Committee discussed that the cap applies to funding associated with student needs including 
special education, poverty, English language learners, and other differentiated aid categories. 
The anticipated reduction in state funding to Manchester was estimated at slightly more than $10 
million annually once the provision takes effect. Members noted that earlier estimates had placed the 
impact closer to $12 million.
September 9, 2026 Committee on Education Legislation 
Page 6 of 7 
 
The Committee discussed pursuing legislation similar to House Bill 1831 to repeal or modify the 
targeted aid cap. 
 
Attorney Upton reported that the Board had scheduled a non-public session for September 24 to 
receive legal guidance regarding the potential for litigation should a legislative remedy not be 
achieved. 
 
The Committee discussed recent statutory changes that place differentiated aid within the broader 
adequacy funding framework. Attorney Upton explained that this could have legal significance 
because reductions to differentiated aid may therefore raise questions regarding the State's 
constitutional responsibility to fund an adequate education. 
 
Members discussed pursuing a legislative remedy as the preferred course while remaining prepared to 
consider legal action if necessary.  They also discussed continued advocacy with the Governor, Mayor, 
state legislators, and organizations involved in school funding issues. 
 
Potential Budget Impact 
The Committee discussed the difficulty the District would face if approximately $10 million in existing 
state funding were eliminated.  Attorney Upton noted that the District has already experienced 
significant position reductions over the past two budget cycles and stated that further reductions of that 
magnitude would be extremely difficult to absorb without affecting District operations.  Members 
discussed the possibility that, absent restoration of the state funding, the financial impact could 
ultimately fall upon Manchester taxpayers or require additional reductions in District expenditures and 
services.  It was emphasized that the District is not seeking new or additional funding through this 
effort, but rather seeking to prevent the loss of funding that is currently provided. 
 
Potential Legal Action and Timeline 
The Committee discussed how the legislative calendar may intersect with the District's annual budget-
development process.  Attorney Upton explained that, if necessary, the District could seek injunctive 
relief to prevent implementation of the funding reduction while a broader legal challenge proceeds. 
Because education funding litigation can take considerable time, the Committee discussed the 
possibility that legal action may need to be initiated before the legislative process is fully resolved.

Attorney Upton indicated that, if sufficient progress toward a legislative remedy is not evident, the 
District may need to consider filing legal action as early as December in order to seek timely injunctive 
relief. 
 
The Committee agreed that both legislative advocacy and potential legal options should continue to be 
evaluated as the implementation date approaches. 
 
  
8. TABLED ITEMS 
 
There were no tabled items this evening. 
 
9.   NEW BUSINESS 
 
No new business was presented.  
 
ADJOURNMENT 
  
10. If there is no further business, a motion is in order to adjourn. 
 
 
On motion of Committee Member Parr, duly seconded by Committee Member Smith, it was moved to 
adjourn.  All were in favor, meeting adjourned at 5:50 p.m.
